utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, yes, as always, I'm ready for my next witness. It is the last background witness, who will also cover areas covered by the indictment. And we are ready to begin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any protective measures for this witness, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please? Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours, for the record the Defence of Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic would like to say happy birthday to our Madam Registrar, Krystal Thompson and happy birthday to Mr. Douglas Stringer who both share the same birthday, that being today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Mr. Krsnik. I hope you could keep the momentum you had last week for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Since last week, our examinations are becoming increasingly concrete in line with the indictment and we will continue to maintain that course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: May I give you a few pieces of advice so that we can carry out this examination-in-chief smoothly? First of all, you see in front of you a screen with the transcript, and you will see a dot moving on the screen. So please pay attention, when the printing stops, then it would be best for you to begin your answer. As we speak the same language, and it needs to be translated into English and French so there should be no overlapping between us. You are testifying according to your own wish in public. Should there be any questions on my part or on the part of the Prosecution that you feel you cannot answer in an open session, there is the institution of a so-called private session. Then you can address yourself to Their Honours and we will go into private session so that the public will not be able to follow. Those are just some general instructions for you.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself very briefly to the Court? Where you were born, your educational background, a brief CV up to 1990, please.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was born in 1960 in a location called Suica in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Ten years later my family moved to Zagreb, where I completed my elementary and secondary schooling and the school of medicine. In 1986, I served in the then Yugoslav People's Army. After that I worked as a medical doctor in a hospital which is some 50 kilometres from Zagreb. That was up to 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now we come to the second part of your CV, with a democratic changes that occurred in 1990 and 1991, so you can tell us the positions that you held and are still holding.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the Croatian democratic union. The party that won at the first elections in Croatia, at the end of 1989, the beginning of 1990, when -- that is in 1990, I was elected deputy to the first parliamentary session after the multi-party elections, and since then, I have been elected to parliament for four mandates. In 1992, I was appointed Secretary-General or rather president of the executive board of the HDZ. In 1993, I -- in September, I became adviser for foreign policy to President Tudjman, a position I held until the President's death. Today, I am a member of the Croatian parliament or Sabor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness for the sake of the record would you please identify yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. That's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You forgot to mention your name, please.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I am Dr. Ivic Pasalic, and everything I have said is my curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let us start with some introductory questions. Let me ask you what I always try to do in my examinations. That is I will insist on your direct knowledge. Things that you personally witnessed or heard or saw. So though my questions will focus on those things, if you do not have direct knowledge, then it is the custom of this Court to accept hearsay evidence as well, but then we have to indicate who is the source, who is the person you heard something from. So my introductory question would be: What was the constitutional order in the Republic of Croatia immediately after its independence in the period 1992-94, therefore?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: After the first elections in Croatia in 1990, the Republic of Croatia was quickly, after that, internationally recognised, and a constitution was adopted according to which Croatia was defined as a country with a semi-presidential constitutional system. So that power was shared, as in all western countries, divided into executive and legislative, and the main pillar of the executive was the government of the Republic of Croatia and the president of the Republic of Croatia in person. That is as far as the executive is concerned? As for the legislative, as for all parliamentary democracies the parliament is the main legislative body in the country. International agreements were approved in parliament. Parliament always debated key issues for the state. In those days, the Croatian parliament was bicameral so that important issues were discussed in both chambers and in view of the difficulties of the times, every effort was made in parliament when the most important issues were on the agenda, to achieve a consensus among all the parliamentary parties, all the parties represented in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which decisions could the President make independently and a subquestion to that, who created and implemented foreign policy?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: According to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pasalic, please slow down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: According to the Croatian constitution, it was clearly defined what the powers of the President of the Republic were. He could independently make a very limited number of decisions. In most cases these were decisions that were made upon the proposal of the government of the Republic of Croatia or decisions which needed to be confirmed in parliament. For example, the President of the Republic would nominate the Prime Minister, but for him to really become the Prime Minister he needed to win the majority -- the approval of the majority in parliament. Or the President of the Republic had the authority to appoint ambassadors but those proposals needed to come from the ministry or rather the Minister of Foreign Affairs. So that there was virtually no decision that the President of the Republic could make autonomously and independently without it having to be approved, either in parliament or that proposal coming in the prior procedure from the government or from the appropriate ministry. With respect to foreign policy, again, pursuant to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, the President of the Republic had those powers and the government of the Republic of Croatia. The government as such, and within the framework of the government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, you were a close associate of the late President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a close associate of President Tudjman and I worked for him as a councillor ever since September, 1993, until the President's death. Before that, I was active in my party, I began collaborating closely with the President in his capacity then as president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have asked you this question because it has been suggested by the Prosecution in this courtroom that President Tudjman was a dictator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's not so, Your Honour we have no position on that issue which is really not relevant to these proceedings, his status. It's our position he was President of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I'll withdraw that question. But then I don't understand, Your Honours, why articles are being produced based on certain allegedly independent sources and then witnesses are asked questions about that. For instance, such a question was put to witness Kovac on the basis of an article in a daily newspaper but never mind, we'll forget that question and I'm glad to hear the position of the Prosecution. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who, in the Republic of Croatia, according to your knowledge, was able to make a decision or had the authority to decide on sending Croatian Army members in an organised manner to another state with the aim of engaging in war operations? The Croatian Army going to the territory of another country to do that, who had such authority?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Such a decision, according to the Croatian constitution, could only have been made by the parliament of the Republic of Croatia or the Sabor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was such a decision ever adopted in the Croatian Sabor? And more specifically, the decision for the Republic of Croatia or rather the Croatian Army to take a direct part in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Such a decision was never made by the Croatian parliament, to send Croatian Army troops outside the territory of Croatia or to engage in any kind of activities outside the borders of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And if the President of the Republic were to make such a decision would it be contrary to the constitution? Would that be a violation of the constitutional order? And who would in such a case, let us assume, let us take -- let us accept a hypothesis that the President may have made such a decision?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Such a decision would be anti-constitutional in the first place, and for violating the constitution, one is held accountable by the constitutional court and there is no doubt that a reaction would have been provoked either by the government of the Republic of Croatia or the Sabor as a whole, and in particular, any political party, especially the opposition parties, which, as in all democracies, monitors closely what the government is doing, especially should it make any serious omissions or act contrary to the constitution. As far as I'm aware, there was never any proceedings conducted in the constitutional court to investigate any decision made by the President of the Republic that would be contrary to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did the Sabor have a debate on this issue?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: There was never any debate in parliament on any instance of violations of the constitution by the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell me, please, did the Sabor adopt any conclusions, to your knowledge, with respect to the behaviour of the Republic of Croatia in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, there was a debate in parliament on this issue, and the latest such debate was in the beginning of January in 1991. And the -- I'm sorry, 2001. And in view of the changed conditions a declaration was adopted by consensus in parliament in which it is explicitly stated that the Republic of Croatia never engaged in any kind of aggressive war, nor did it commit aggression against any other state. In fact, it was emphasised that the Republic of Croatia engaged in a defensive war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It's the declaration on the homeland war of the 13th of October, 2000. I have provided Their Honours with a copy of this declaration. Do you have -- are you aware that President Tudjman supervised or designated anyone in the Republic of Croatia to directly interfere in the military operations and activities of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Object to the leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware that President Tudjman may have directly designated someone to supervise or plan operations of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, it's the same question, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to put your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. Maybe I'll leave it out. It doesn't occur to me how to put it in more general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, just say to him generally what was President Tudjman's position in relation to the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You have heard the question. So please answer it, if you can.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: In relation to the Croatian Army --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. What was his position in relation to the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: The President of the Republic is the Commander-in-Chief of the Croatian Army, according to the constitution, and as such, he had all the powers stipulated by the law and the constitution. In the chain of command, he was the Minister of the Defence and the Chief of the Main Staff, but the operative command authority was in the hands of the President of the Republic and the Chief of the Main Staff. The President of the Republic, pursuant to the constitution and the law, appointed officers, relieved officers, gave decorations, awards. That was more or less the position of the President in relation to the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How were ranks awarded, according to your own knowledge, ranks in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: As an adviser for home policy, I was not responsible for those matters, nor did I -- was I involved in those activities. All I know is that that was the responsibility of other people in the first place of the Minister of Defence, and the staff of the President's military cabinet. The procedure of awarding of ranks is regulated by the constitution and the law, and concisely, upon the proposal of the Chief of Staff or the Defence Minister, the President of the Republic would issue a decree on military appointments and the awarding of ranks, especially high-level officers' ranks. I don't know about the lower ranks, lower level ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, tell me now, generally, the position of President Tudjman as the Commander-in-Chief in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina? I hope this is not leading now.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I have nothing to say about that, as Bosnia-Herzegovina is another state, and the President of the Republic of Croatia had no authority in relation to that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did he interfere in any way in the activities of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, as far as you are aware, did the Republic of Croatia directly and in a decisive manner participate in the conflict between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia did not in any way take part, never mind in a decisive manner in the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This conflict or any other conflict that may have occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Quite on the contrary, the policies of the Republic of Croatia and the policies of President Tudjman, was to establish and promote peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to halt the war, to stop the suffering, for a whole series of reasons. In any war, and especially in that war, there were very high casualties. This destabilised the entire region. The Republic of Croatia had direct and indirect damages due to everything that was happening, through the Republic of Croatia, hundreds of thousands of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina passed. The wounded from Bosnia-Herzegovina were treated in Croatian hospitals regardless of whether they were Croats or Muslims. So it was in the interests of the Republic of Croatia that peace be restored in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me continue with this group of questions and ask you very concretely and very directly whether you have any knowledge as to whether the Republic of Croatia may have participated in the planning and the supervision of military operations in the conflict that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, although we already discussed that issue. Do you know if there was a decision made at any point in time about sending the Croatian Army to Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to participate in conflicts with Muslims and take territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina that would subsequently belong exclusively to the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, the Republic of Croatia never prepared or planned or supervised any military operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And secondly, never did the Republic of Croatia plan or implement any military operations against or towards Bosnia and Herzegovina in the way you put it, in order to occupy an area or to win it exclusively for the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So these two allegations are absolutely -- cannot be -- I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were there any special relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially with regard to the provisions of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia? Was there any exclusivity in the relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: According to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia I believe it's Article 10 of the Croatian constitution, the Republic of Croatia is obliged to look after Croats who live outside Croatia, and especially of those Croats who are particularly threatened. The Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, together with the Republic of Croatia for that matter, were the victims of the greatest Serbian aggression. They went through all sorts of suffering. And in that sense, the Republic of Croatia did look after them by sending them humanitarian aid, by looking after them, after those who were expelled from their homes, and this was the type of relationship and the type of assistance that was given to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know how many Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina live in the Republic of Croatia, who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: There are different statistical sources but the rough number is about 300.000 to 350.000 people altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know why the international negotiations about Bosnia and Herzegovina involved the late Franjo Tudjman? Why did he participate in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: There is a whole number of reasons, and the key reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have to warn you, we have another translation -- interpretation into French for the honourable Judge Diarra, so can you please slow down for the sake of that translation?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: So the key reason for which President Tudjman participated in the peace negotiations about the resolution of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina was at the request by the international community. The second reason was that the Republic of Croatia, as a state, was interested in the restoration of peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The third reason was that the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina very often in these negotiations gave President Tudjman the power of attorney to negotiate on their behalf. All of these three reasons could be explained at length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik can I interrupt and ask a question that's troubling me at this stage? This witness was a very young doctor in 1992 and 1993. You haven't laid any foundation as to how he is now giving evidence to us, how he's qualified to talk about what President Tudjman's military operations were. We -- I'm becoming increasingly disturbed about the testimony which he's giving which sounds like he's an expert on constitutional law, on military law and the military relations between the two parties. Perhaps you can put my mind at ease on that. For instance, what did Dr. Pasalic actually advise Dr. Tudjman on in 1992 and 1993? It could have been on the health situation or setting up of hospitals for all we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Clark, we will come to all that and we will give you the foundation for this testimony, because Mr. Pasalic was a close associate for eight years of President Tudjman's and he spent -- he would spend entire days working along with President Tudjman. I attended a number of meetings with international participation, meetings at a local level, and if there is anybody who is to give evidence on that, it is Dr. Pasalic. That's why the Defence has asked Dr. Pasalic to come here and to clarify some issues. He is the person who has the foundations to testify about that. He interrupted his medical career in 1992, when he became the Secretary-General of the HDZ and in 1993, the closest associate of the late president and he discharged this duty every day, day in, day out, for the following eight years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President we are grateful for counsel's clarification. We share the views expressed by Judge Clark about the foundation for what the witness is testifying about. I don't have any reason to disagree with the resume that's just been given by Mr. Krsnik but I suggest that we do need to it hear about this from the witness rather than in the form of testimony from Mr. Krsnik. The witness really hasn't told us any of the things about himself that we just heard from Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you may ask some specific questions concerning those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours, but I thought that Dr. Pasalic's CV was clear enough, what he said in the introduction, but obviously we can ask him a few questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All these things we have discussed so far, and that we are going to discuss from now on, where did you get all this knowledge from? Is this your personal knowledge, you've heard Judge Clark and you have heard the Prosecutor. So can you clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Certainly, with pleasure. As I've already stated, in 1990, I was elected deputy in the Croatian parliament, the Sabor, and ever since, I have participated in the political life of Croatia. In 1992, in September of 1992, I was appointed the President of the executive board of the HDZ. That is a duty which corresponds to the duty of the general secretary -- Secretary-General of a party, and I cooperated closely, day in, day out, with President Tudjman, because besides being the President of the state, he was also the President of the party. In that capacity, I participated in a number of meetings and from 1993, the September of 1993, onwards, I discharged the duty of the adviser on home affairs, on internal affairs, and in that capacity, I cooperated with President Tudjman on a daily basis, until his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How many personal meetings did you have, eye to eye, with the President, and in how many -- at how many meetings did you participate during that period of seven to eight years?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to give you the number of these meetings that I had with President Tudjman. There must have been hundreds or thousands of meetings, because every day I would spend 12 days in the office, sometimes even longer, so I would very often meet with President Tudjman and those meetings were daily, regular operational meetings. Some of them were shorter, some of them took longer so during that period of eight years there must have been thousands of such meetings. As regards official meetings, I believe that I have attended hundreds of them. I have never counted them. I have never maintained any statistics, but I know that there were a number of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Besides attending these meetings personally, in any capacity, either as an active participant or a passive participant, you also had confidential meetings and talks with the late president and discussed various issues. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: My duty was such that I had to discuss confidential issues with the late president very often. These were the issues of the most confidential nature and they pertained to my duties as the adviser for the home affairs and on the other hand, the procedures and the manner of work in the Office of the President were such that every day we would lunch together so this was a very -- lunch organised in a close, intimate circle of associates and it was always a working lunch, and this is where we discussed various issues, exchanged information. So that it was only logical that as the adviser for internal affairs, I was briefed on a number of issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I ask you something, Dr. Pasalic, just to put my mind at ease while I'm listening to this evidence. In 1993 and 1994, were you a frequent attender when the events in Herzegovina especially that's what we are interested in, Herzegovina, were raised by the President with Mr. Susak, the late minister for defence? Would you have been a regular attender at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did attend some of these meetings. I can't say that I was at all of these meetings, because the President of the Republic had the -- made a note of all of these meetings and he invited to these meetings the officials that he wanted to invite, and it is very hard for me to say, to give you the percentage of these meetings that I attended, but, yes, I did attend a number, a certain number of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I ask you a further question, Dr. Pasalic? When the late President Tudjman had meetings with generals from the army and with Mr. Susak, would it be normal for you also to be included in the list of attendees at those meetings when they were talking about the progress or otherwise of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to military issues, I was a rarely invited to such meetings. Sometimes I would be attending such meetings but that was rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I think you understand my concerns, that the type of evidence this witness is giving when he is clearly not an expert on those matters. Perhaps you would confine his evidence to the areas that he is totally at home with and he would have been a special adviser to Dr. Tudjman on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe we should clarify matters completely. I shall ask questions instead of giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact whether you attended these meetings or not, did the President discuss things with you? Did he inform you about the things which happened at the meetings? Did he confide in you? Did he ask for your opinion regardless of the type of the meetings? In your daily contacts, that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to object to the first part of that string of questions, as leading. I think that there are some aspects which are leading but I think I can just withdraw it and allow the witness to go ahead, to try to frame an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear what the witness is going to tell us. Witness, you may answer that question put by the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when it comes to the important political issues, and the issues of the state policy, as I have already said, I had a number of working meetings with President Tudjman, very many tete-a-tete meetings, and as regards important issues, even the issues which fell beyond the scope of my advisory duty, I was informed to the extent it was needed, i.e. to the extent to which it was important for me to know about the most important things that were happening in the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me move on. You have heard the doubts about -- as to what specific questions you should be asked. So let me be more concrete and tell you, and ask you that if you do not have any personal knowledge, you can tell us, "No, I don't have." If you do, please tell us, "Yes, I was attending such and such meeting or I discussed the issue with the late president." So let's be more specific. Did you personally or in any of your conversations with the late president, could say something about the allegation that we heard here in the courtroom and that is that President Tudjman, the HDZ and even the Republic of Croatia determined positions, run political moves, of the HZ HB or the HR HB?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to the question as leading, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that you have to take this witness step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why my direct examination is being interrupted so often today. I have invited this witness because of the position that he has held, and I wanted to -- him to be my last background witness, because this witness has a lot of knowledge about what happened in the late President Tudjman's office, things that are very often referred to in this courtroom. If my questions have been leading, I'm going to rephrase them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So let me ask you this: According to your knowledge, did anybody have any influence on the political or any other issues in the HZ HB or HR HB?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were organised either as the HZ HB and later on HR HB, and their key top officials who discharged various duties were absolutely autonomous in their decisions, be it the personnel decisions or political decisions. In some crisis situations, situations of the peace negotiations, I remember that on several occasions, representatives of the international community asked President Tudjman to exert his influence on the personnel changes because they considered some people unacceptable, either because of the fact that they were contaminated by the war events or they were perceived as the persons who provoked the opposite side, and it is only in this context that one can talk about a certain influence that the President of the Republic of Croatia had. I know several such examples but in all of these cases, it was only the matter of the President putting forth his opinion, his position, which only served to speed up the peace process in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but even under these circumstances, he did not have any power to order somebody to do something. That was absolutely impossible. But due to the fact that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina respected President Tudjman as a person, that they trusted him, that in the peace negotiations he very often had their mandate to negotiate on their behalf, his proposals and his opinions were accepted as such in several situations that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the resignation of Mr. Mate Boban and what brought to that resignation? Do you have any personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: What I personally know about that is that in the early 1994, Mate Boban resigned from the duties that he had discharged up to then. In a conversation with the President, and in a conversation with some international representatives at some meetings that I attended, Mr. Boban was directly asked to resign because he was in a way a symbol of the war events and as such was an obstacle to the -- to reaching the peace agreement. When the President discussed that with Mr. Boban, the latter did not accept these arguments, i.e., he -- it was his opinion that Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Silajdzic and Mr. Ganic and some other top military officials should have resigned along the line of the same arguments. He did not want that to be only unilateral because he believed that this would not contribute towards the peace process, i.e., that it would provoke resistance in the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I believe that after some time, when the pressure became even more -- even stronger, that it was then that Mr. Boban finally resigned, at a Sabor or rally of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was relieved of his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Pasalic, as far as you can remember, did you personally attend meetings where the representatives of the international community in the Office of the President or elsewhere which meetings were these, if you can remember, and what was the position of the international community you have now told us their position about Mate Boban but what were the positions about the peace processes, whether this was an active position or passive position? What were their general positions on the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e., on the peace process?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: There were a number of such conversations and meetings, a number of them which took place abroad. So very many of them abroad, very many of them in Croatia. I did not attend any of the meetings abroad, because other officials attended those meetings. I participated in a number of talks that -- which took place in the Office of the President of the Republic, or in some other places in the Republic of Croatia. Representatives of the international community were actively involved in various forms of peace negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, would you please be so kind and name people? When you say, when one says the international community, it is nameless. Can you please mention any of the names of the people who actually attended these meetings, what did they say, what was the course of these talks, regarding the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I can give you the names but as for the details of this -- these talks, I would kindly ask you if we could go into private session because some of the -- my knowledge about the details of who said what, I believe, are confidential and fall under the confidentiality of the duties that I discharged. So when it comes to the names of these people, I can say, tell the names of these people openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into the private session? Because as I believe you have the duty to keep the state secret. Is that the reason why you are asking for the private session?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly the reason, because the delicate data which are secret, we have to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So can you please give us the names and as for the details we will move into the private session?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: The peace negotiators were Mr. Owen, Mr. Vance, Mr. Stoltenberg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what is your personal knowledge and were you personally present at meetings between Dr. Tudjman and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic? What was their relationship? Did it change? What do you personally know about it?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I was present at a number of such meetings. I think a couple were held in Zagreb and I think I was in Sarajevo once or twice with the President, with President Tudjman. President Tudjman accepted and respected Mr. Izetbegovic as the leader of the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was aware that he was the key figure for achieving peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as regards the Muslims. Unfortunately, on the other hand, and we discussed this quite often, he was disappointed by the way in which Mr. Izetbegovic was behaving. Namely, he changed his opinions very often, especially after certain agreements would be reached or certain solutions agreed upon, and President Tudjman was disappointed precisely because he was a man who held to his word. He considered agreements to be binding, and Mr. Izetbegovic would agree on one thing and even sign something, whereas in practice, and on the ground, they acted differently. And this was something that President Tudjman was deeply annoyed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know whether this relationship between them changed or did he continue to have this attitude of respect for Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: In spite of everything, President Tudjman continued to have respectful attitude towards Mr. Izetbegovic, and I think that this was after the Dayton agreements were reached, it went so far that President Tudjman wishing to demonstrate in that way too how keen he was on there being, in spite of everything, confidence between Muslims and Croats in particular, President Tudjman awarded the highest Croatian decoration to President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have another five minutes until the break, so let me try and round off this topic with the question: Do you personally know, and what is your personal knowledge about, the so-called, I'm going to use the word famous or infamous, napkin of Paddy Ashdown? This is Exhibit P796. And could the usher please show Mr. Pasalic this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could the English version be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we only have an English version. There is no Croatian version. Could the usher place the other, much more important, exhibit on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you talk to the President, or rather what do you personally know about this napkin? Let me ask you first, do you recognise Mr. Tudjman's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know President Tudjman's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is it this his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No this is not President Tudjman's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What do you personally know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I discussed with President Tudjman this incident on a number of occasions, and he was saddened but more than that, because he said it was inconceivable to him what people are prepared to make up and lie about, especially people that he had met during the celebrations of the victory of the antifascist coalition, highly respectable people. So he found it strange that Mr. Ashdown should have made this story public and I asked the President what happened at that luncheon and did he write anything on this napkin because I found it quite unbelievable, and he said that he was really sorry that anyone could make up something like that, and that he had only tried to explain to the gentleman something that can be found in all professional magazines and that is the map from 1992 and 1993, the line of separation, which was drawn by NATO circles, that is the separation between east and west Europe. And he said to me that he had tried to explain to this gentleman that this kind of line was drawn probably with the idea that some global solution should be sought along those lines, but it was quite outside any context of the division of Bosnia or any other land. These were simply professional arguments about things that are far beyond the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the former Yugoslavia or the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, 1995, on that day, in fact, did the army of the Republic of Croatia and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in those days, were they acting together? They were allies in the war. What is the meaning of this story dating back to the 6th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: In those days, there was -- I'm sorry, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Because all military conflicts ceased by then. Croatia had been occupied almost a third of its territory but there were no military conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it is time for the break. Perhaps before the break, I could show this map on the ELMO. This whole booklet is being translated so could we just place this map on the ELMO? I hope my learned friends won't mind. I will have a copy ready for you when I receive the translation. Could the usher please assist and show this map. We do have an exhibit number, ID D1/400. I'm still waiting for the translation. I hope it will be ready in the course of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you please be kind enough and tell me, do you recognise this map? Is this the map published by NATO headquarters in Brussels with this separation line?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this map on President Tudjman. I don't know the exact name of the book but that is the map I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will resume at 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let us now move on to another topic, again I shall be asking you about your own personal knowledge. Tell me, was there a difference between the policy of the state and the policy of the HDZ as a party in the Republic of Croatia, or could we place an equation sign between the two?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: There was the party policy, and of course the policy of the country. I think that it goes without saying that every party has its own programme, its objectives, its methods of political struggle, and state policy, though it varies from situation to situation, and the balance of forces in parliament, but in our particular case, there were differences between state policies and narrow party policies, as President Tudjman would often indicate. So I think there is no dilemma when the policies of the party were defined, party members would be involved exclusively, whereas in the creation of state policies, state officials would be involved, and in various stages of the development of government, there were members of government that were not members of the HDZ. In fact belonged to other parties. So that in defining state policies, experts were often invited to participate. That is people who were not party members. As for parliament, where many important issues were debated, proceeding from the definition of key state policies, beyond the narrow legislative frameworks, there were attempts to achieve consensus, especially in view of the backdrop of the war that was ongoing, so that very frequently, questions that were important for the state of Croatia, a consensus was sought and achieved so that that would be the state policy and not party policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me what you personally know about the relationship with the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was it a special kind of relationship? Who defined that relationship, who determined their policies? A little about that.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: The HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina developed as an independent party, as one of the parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It came into being as democracy was making its initial steps in the former Yugoslavia. Their documents and their registration were regulated by the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and within the framework of their programme objectives, they pursued their party policies. The HDZ of Croatia was an independent party in the Republic of Croatia. With regard to the relationship between the two parties, I can say that that relationship was based on the similarity between our two parties, in terms of programmes, similar to what in democracies you have social democratic parties, people's parties, so that the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a related party to the HDZ of Croatia, but in terms of personnel policy, decision-making and everything else, they were and remained two separate parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, let me now move on to the so-called transcripts produced in the President's office. So again, will you limit your remarks to your personal knowledge? My first question is: What do you personally know about the conversations that were recorded, those that were not and in general terms what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I can say that certain conversations in the President's office were recorded, in the first place, international contacts by the President of the Republic, and it was an unwritten rule, as everywhere else, that talks of that nature should be recorded. Secondly, official meetings of state bodies chaired by the President of the Republic were also recorded. And this was obligatory, daily operative talks, tete-a-tete talks of the President with us, who would spend several hours with him on a daily basis. Those were not recorded. That would be an answer in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the people attending those meetings, are they informed that they are being recorded?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: The people coming from abroad, they were senior state officials, and they knew that this was part of the protocol, part of the regular procedure. As for meetings with the domestic participants, President Tudjman, who chaired those meetings would usually in the course of the meeting warn somebody and say, "Please introduce yourself for the transcript." So this was customary. At the beginning of the meeting, no one would say, "This meeting is going to be recorded." But while chairing the meeting the President would say something to that effect, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: As far as you know, were copies of the transcript given for authorisation, authentication?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, copies were never distributed for authentication purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were copies of the transcript given to anyone at all for any purpose?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, copies were not made, nor were they given to anyone. If there should be a need for any reason whatsoever, if somebody wanted to read the transcript for some reason, then the procedure to obtain the original would be for the person to read them in the chief of cabinet's office and return it to him immediately afterwards. I'm not aware that it was ever possible for anyone to have a copy of that transcript or for that transcript to be copied at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In 1991, were you in the President's office?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, I was not in the President's office at the time. I was a deputy at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the possibility of a copy of the transcript being distributed in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I can only answer on the basis of my conversations with people who were chiefs of cabinet. There were only two persons in that position, and on the basis of my conversations with those two persons regarding procedures in general, the protocol that was observed in the Office of the President, it was never the practice for copies of the transcript to be made or to be distributed to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know who was chief of cabinet in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I think it was Mrs. Zdravka Busic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And if a copy were to be given, who would be responsible for that? Let us assume that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: The permission to do such a thing would have to be given by the President of the Republic, and then the actual act would be carried out by the chief of cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Exclusively?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively the chief of cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have asked you all these questions because in another trial, a witness claimed that a transcript was given to him by President Tudjman, and that is why I felt it necessary to ask you about the procedure and the official who would be responsible for this. And this happened to be a transcript from 1991. Let us move on now. Do you know whether we have just heard what you said about copies but was there any authentication ever?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, what you personally know about who was in charge, let us call it the archives. Who was in charge of those transcripts emanating from conversations in the President's office?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: That was the responsibility of the chief of cabinet of the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was it possible to make any handwritten notes on those transcripts?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would it be possible for pages of transcripts to be missing? Who would check these things, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Something like that, as far as I know, is simply not possible, because of the procedure applied with respect to those transcripts. It was impossible for pages to go missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, would it be possible for such transcripts from meetings in the President's office not to indicate the name of the speaker?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. That was not possible, because the technology was such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you please describe to Their Honours the actual procedure?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: There were two rooms in the office where meetings were held and recorded. That is official meetings. There was a big room, a big office, and another one somewhat smaller, adjacent to the President's cabinet where he worked. There were microphones on the desks and there was a room in the President's -- within the President's office which housed the recording equipment. There was a technician who was in charge of that, and when the meeting started or during the course of the meeting, depending on the technical capabilities, a transcript of the meeting would be done. As soon as the transcript was completed, the technician would send the transcript to the chief of cabinet. The chief of cabinet would put a state secret on the envelope and he would file the transcript away. In brief, that was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So every transcript -- a transcript for certain meeting, would be sealed in an envelope so the envelope would be closed and marked with the degree of confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: All meetings which were recorded were recorded following the same procedure. The transcript would be sealed in an envelope. The envelope would be marked with the "state secret."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is that the highest degree of confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: According to the Croatian law, this is the highest of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who had access to the archives? Who was in charge of the archives?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: The access was rather limited and reduced to the chief of cabinet, obviously, he, whenever accessed the archives it would be with the permission of the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with these transcripts after President Tudjman's death?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that only on the basis of what I heard in my conversations with the people who were in charge of that part of work. After the death of the President of the Republic, the government issued a decree on handling these transcripts and all other documents which at that time were in the President's office. By that decree issued by the government in late 1999, the whole bulk of the documentation was grouped in three groups, into documents that arose from the work of the President as a statesman. The second group was the documentation that was his documentation as the President of the party. And the third was his personal documentation. The third group should have been stored in the office for national security. The first part, that is. The party documentation should have been taken over by HDZ officials and the private documentation should have been handed to the family of the late President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you ever testified in front of any body regarding transcripts from President Tudjman's office and the authenticity of these transcripts?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I have testified before the Croatian parliament. I have testified before the parliamentary commission which was dealing with the privatisation of a daily paper in Croatia. And one of the documents which was discussed and about which I testified were papers which were represented to me as a witness as transcripts from the Office of President Tudjman. The commission, after having heard all the witnesses, refused to accept this document, disputing its authenticity. The same documents were later on used by some state bodies. I believe this was the state Attorney General, and the transcript or the papers which looked like a transcript, again were rejected as not being authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know why did they appear in the media? Were you personally involved in the media regarding these transcripts?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: When the new President of the Republic was elected, the Croatian media were swarming with various papers which were allegedly transcripts from the Office of the President of the Republic. What I found very strange was that one or some of these transcripts contained conversations between President Tudjman and myself, tete-a-tete. And there were also conversations between President Tudjman and some other people, again tete-a-tete meetings, private meetings. In the case of my alleged conversations it was clear that it was a forgery because my conversations were never recorded, nor were working meetings ever recorded, that is meetings between the President and us who worked in his office. Some other persons also filed charges in order to dispute the authenticity of such papers and only recently, in a procedure, the Judge refused to accept these documents as not being authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What is the role of the person who actually gave these documents to the media? Who gave them this document -- these documents? Has that resulted in any new laws being passed by the current government as a result of all the doubts about the authenticity of these documents?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you what has appeared in the media and what the current President of the Republic has told the media. It is obvious that it was him who gave these papers to the media because that is what the journalists have said, but he himself has also said that he would furnish the media with these documents for as long as there is any interest in having these documents. Pressure was made on the people who, for various reasons, were considered to be the late president's opponents, his political opponents. As soon as something like that appeared in the press, a few days later, documents would appear to discredit such persons, being politicians or athletes. I'm not going to go into the reasons of the government, I suppose that they had their reasons and I suppose the government issued a decree to the effect of all the documentation arising from the Office of the President of the Republic which was compiled during the -- President Tudjman's tenure should be transferred into the archives of the state without actually establishing whether these documents are authentic or not. So much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And how can one know now where the authentic transcripts are? An issue has been raised here regardless of whether this is confidential or not, but it would help this Court to establish whether some of the documents are actually authentic. How is it possible today to establish that the authenticity of these documents, you were there, you would probably know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness it's my understanding so far he's been testifying about things that he learned from other people after the death of President Tudjman, at which time I believe the witness no longer held his position within the government of Croatia so what he knows is what other people told him after he was no longer part of the government, or what he knows is information that he's read in the media, from what I can gather from his testimony. So on this particular point, it's not clear that a foundation has been laid for the witness to give evidence as to the -- whether the transcripts in an authentic or correct fashion, can be found at any particular place. I don't know what he knows about that at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I quite agree with you on your argument but this Trial Chamber would like to hear what this witness is going to tell us about the authenticity of those documents. We'll give the proper weight to his testimony at a later stage. Witness, you may answer that question put by the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have told you what I know from my personal knowledge and one of those things is the testimony and the debate before the parliamentary body, and the papers which were referred to as transcripts were rejected by that same parliamentary body as not being authentic. So this is my direct knowledge and experience illustrated by one example. Secondly, I know that in a trial before a court, a Judge also refused to accept these so-called transcripts as authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I ask a question, Dr. Pasalic while we are on that. Because it might be several hours before I come back and we'll have lost its value. What was the issue that was actually being determined by the parliamentary commission? Was it the transcripts in general or a particular portion which had been shown to them? We need to know what the commission was determining.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The task of that commission was to establish the circumstances around the sale of a daily paper in Croatia, and one of the documents which were considered were the papers which did look like transcripts from the present of the state's office. They were presented as transcripts which were to serve to prove a certain fact. The parliamentary commission refused to accept these papers as authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do I understand from that, Dr. Pasalic, that the main issue which was being determined was the sale of a daily newspaper and a side issue was a selection of documents which purported to be or had been held out by that newspaper to be original transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So one of the key documents which were considered during that procedure was to establish the possible credibility of the papers or the so-called transcripts. That was one of the key issues. So the parliamentary commission, and later on the -- a judiciary body, refused to accept these papers, the so-called transcripts, as authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I may not have expressed myself very clearly, Dr. Pasalic. I think I asked you, certainly I meant to ask you, whether the main issue was the sale of the newspaper and the side issue was a selection of documents which purported to be transcripts. I want you to be quite clear about my question. I'm asking you, can you make a distinction between the transcripts in general, the entire body of the transcripts, as being true documents, and documents which were used by the newspaper and purported to be from the archive of the transcripts? Do you see the distinction? One is the authenticity of the general transcripts which you appear to have verified any way that they were existed, they were made, they were kept, and the side issue a selection of documents which were rejected by the commission. Could you clarify that for me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try and be more precise. So the main issue in the work of that parliamentary body was the sale of a daily paper. So that was the main issue discussed. Within the decision on that main issue, one of the arguments or a piece of evidence or proof, was a paper that was presented as a transcript. In making the decision on the main issue, the parliamentary decision rejected that paper, that document, as not being authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So the parliamentary commission, as I understand you now, did not make any determination on the validity, authenticity or otherwise of the vast body of documents known as the presidential transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because it was not its duty. On that particular occasion, it was given just one paper, that was presented as transcript. It did not discuss or consider or made a decision on the body of the transcripts, because it was not its task. It was not its duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Could I just ask you one question because obviously it's very important for us arising out of that. Was the one paper which the commission declared to be unauthentic, was that paper a document that's relied upon, if you know, in this trial? If you don't know that, can you tell us what the paper was about so that we know that we are ad idem on the findings of the commission and the documents that we are considering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commission was determining the suspicion about illegal acts that may have occurred during the sale of a daily newspaper, and these papers suggested that the President of the state played a role in that transaction. And the -- the parliamentary commission refused this piece of paper as not being authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was that -- that was the commission related to a paper that has nothing whatever to do with the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, in relation to the Court's determination, you referred to two determinations in relation to documents which purported to come from the parliamentary -- sorry, the presidential transcripts, one being the commission and the second one being a court determination recently. Do you know what that particular document was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the second case, I can only tell you about this document, what was published in the Croatian media. It was a trial, a court trial, in which a former Croatian official was brought to trial under the suspicion that he committed some illegal acts, and the key argument to prove that were papers which were presented as transcripts. The judge refused to accept these papers as authentic. So she refused to accept them as evidence in the court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If we were to try and establish or try and obtain a copy of that court order, how would we go about it? When was that decision made and at what level of court was it made by? Was it investigating magistrate? Was it a constitutional court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was some ten days ago, and the Court was -- it was a regular court proceedings before the municipal court in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you remember, I have already announced that I have already asked for that decision. I'm waiting for this decision to be brought to me, and this was not a municipal court but the county court in Zagreb but this is not the only decision. There are several such decisions. But I was going to inform the Honourable Court with that any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Forgive me for taking over. This is my last question now and I'll let you get on. It's just appropriate. Otherwise it gets lost in the re-examination. Are decisions of the county court subject to appeal in Croatia? Do they operate like they do in other countries, before it's finalised so many weeks have to go by?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It's subject to appeal, so in other words it's not a final order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is not a final order. It's subject to it appeal. And we are impatiently awaiting that, because our appeals are two instance appeals and I believe that the matter will be finally adjudicated by the Supreme Court of Croatia because the general public also waits for the resolution of that enigma, and this has brought me to the end of my investigation. I apologise, Your Honours. My colleague is suggesting that I ask something else. Actually he reminds me to ask whether recently you have heard anything about the initiative of the group of parliamentarians in the Croatian parliament, the initiative to establish a new parliamentary commission that would deal with nothing else but the presidential transcripts?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Tomorrow, preparations start for the new regular session of the Croatian parliament. And one of the items on the agenda is the establishment of an investigation commission, investigative committee, that will deal with nothing but the presidential transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be all from me, Dr. Pasalic. Thank you for coming here and thank you for helping this Court to it make an objective picture of the time that is the topic of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If I had known that Dr. Pasalic was at the end of his evidence, I wouldn't have interrupted I'm really sorry to both of you for asking so many questions but I thought you had many more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have given my questions to my colleague Krsnik and he has actually been the one to ask them. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Cross-examination, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, we do have some documents that we wanted to use during the cross-examination, and we have in the courtroom binders and copies that we could distribute to counsel and to the Trial Chamber and the registry. And I need to get organised. Could I suggest that we take an early break now and then come back? It may than we could simply go through to the end of the day today, and I could complete the cross-examination today. But that during the break we could distribute all of the materials and really save the time that we would be taking now to do that. I'm in your hands, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well we could take an early break but you have to finish the cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm confident that I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume at --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, I don't have anything against an early break but I would like the Prosecutor to use as much time as I used in the direct examination, because I would like to leave the Honourable Court sometime for their questions, because I'm -- I believe that we certainly have to finish by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at ten minutes past 5.00. --- Break taken at 4.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Mr. President, a procedural matter and I appreciate the Chamber giving me a moment. In terms of the lineup of witnesses for the rest of the week, it appears that possibly we may be picking up some speed. We were given as the Chamber may know some names last week, as the Court had directed the Defence to do. However, after this witness, perhaps, Your Honour, it would be simplest and save time if we just went into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 12232 to 12244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer, your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P930, please? It's in the binder that was just distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, there are a number of papers that I'm going to ask you to look at during the course of your cross-examination, they are in this binder. Organised numerically, chronologically at the bottom of the first page of each Exhibit you'll find an Exhibit number with a P in front of it. Perhaps the usher could find you -- or assist you in finding Exhibit P930.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic while he's doing that, I can tell you what this is. We got this off of your web site. You have a web site, I understand, www Ivic Pasalic dot-com; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I have, according to the CV we have here you're fluent in English and in fact the CV we pulled off your web site is in fact in the English language. That's it.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I understand English quite well but I can't say that I speak it fluently. So I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, it says on your CV that you're fluent in English so you might want to have them change that. Just looking at this, sir, it appeared to me, appears to me that you were born in a place called Suica in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I understand that is located in the region or in the municipality of Tomislavgrad, is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were trained as a medical doctor and I see that, among the medical experience that you have is that you have been a doctor, a physician, at the correctional facility in Zagreb and have been, in fact, the director of that facility in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: For three months, I was in charge of that facility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that the facility where Mladen Naletilic was held subsequently in 1997 to 1999 before he was transferred to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: There is only one prison hospital in Zagreb. I don't know exactly where Mr. Naletilic was, if he was in Zagreb this is the only hospital of a correctional facility in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Subsequently, when you were a member of President Tudjman's -- when you were one of his advisers, did you ever go to meet Mr. Naletilic when he was being held at the prison in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that yes or no or you just are simply unable to recall?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, I did not visit Mr. Naletilic. If I had, I would remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Not in a personal or in an official capacity, then?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Have you ever met him before, in any place?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have occasion to meet Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You have been, it's my understanding, a member of the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ in Croatia, essentially since the time it was founded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I have been a member of the HDZ since the end of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you have been a member of the Croatian parliament or the Sabor essentially continuously, on a continuous basis since you were first elected in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I was elected to the Croatian Sabor in all its sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as of today, sir, you're still a sitting member of the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
