utterances.text: Now, it's my understanding, sir, that recently, you were a candidate for the position of President of the HDZ of Croatia but that you were unsuccessful in your bid to take that position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was a candidate for the Presidency of the HDZ, and I won 47 per cent of the votes, whereas my opposing candidate got 51 per cent of the votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And really, I think the most significant for our purposes is the fact that you were what sounds to me to be an important councillor or adviser to President Tudjman during the years 1992 to the time of his death in late 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. I was appointed adviser to the President of the Republic in September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the sphere of your responsibilities was to be an adviser or a counsellor to the President in matters involving domestic or home affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that during the time that you were an adviser, President Tudjman's adviser on internal affairs that were you in fact an opponent and opposed to Croatia's cooperating with this organisation, this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. When we in Croatia in parliament, discussed the adoption of a law on cooperation with the International criminal Tribunal, I was one of those who played an important role in the adoption of that law, because among the Croatian public and within my party, there were certain reservations with respect to the adoption of that law, and at the time, in parliament, I urged that the law be adopted, though personally I had my doubts as to whether it was the best solution. And in parliament, I believe I played an important role in the adoption of that law, hoping and believing that the role of this Tribunal, as we saw it at the time, would be fulfilled, and that meant that all those who have committed serious war crimes should be held responsible for those crimes. Also, we firmly believed that facts would be adhered to, the truth would be upheld, with respect to everything that occurred in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and in particular, that crimes would be punished that occurred in -- within the framework of the greater Serbian aggression against the Republic of Croatia. That was my position when the constitutional law on cooperation was being adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Subsequently sir you've spoken and been highly critical of the Tribunal in its efforts to investigate, for example, Croatian generals who were in charge of the operations called Storm and Flash. Haven't you been opposed to Croatia's cooperation with the Tribunal in respect of Storm and Flash?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: In the Croatian parliament, we had debates on that issue, and my position at the time was, and still is today, that it is my belief that there are legal arguments leading to doubts as to whether the International Criminal Tribunal is responsible for the Storm and Flash operations. While the HDZ was in power, at the legal level, we presented arguments calling that in question, and that was the position of the HDZ while we were in power. That is there were doubts as to whether this Tribunal is the place to deal with these two operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, did you say in December of 1998 that, "It would certainly put into question Croatia's cooperation with the Tribunal, all the way to possible annulment of Croatia's law on cooperation with the Tribunal should Croatia's top generals be indicted by this Tribunal"? Were those your words, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the quotation is quite correct, but it would be much simpler if you have a document indicating that I said that. Then I would be able to answer your question quite directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Exhibit 581.01, sir, I think if you go back toward the front of the binder, what I have, sir, is an article from a publication called the Feral Tribune. In this article which is actually an article or an editorial written by someone named Banac, in this article, sir, that very quote is attributed to you as having been a statement that you gave to a different periodical called Jutarnji List. Exhibit 851.01.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to this question, because it would be fairer to the witness to show him that newspaper. Vecernji List, not a commentary of another journalist commenting on something that somebody else had written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that this witness has the full right to recognise what he said or deny what he did not say. This is a newspaper article. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you have to indicate on which page this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic, I can point you if you look at me, the very bottom of the last column the part I highlighted that contains the quotes I'm asking you about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The English version, Mr. President, it is the last full paragraph, I'm sorry, the second to last full paragraph on the second page of the English translation. I'll read it again, sir, and perhaps you'll be able to follow along with me. It's reported, and this is the quote: "If Croatian generals will really be called to The Hague, it is entirely sure that our patience will be brought to an end. That will certainly bring into question Croatian cooperation with The Hague Tribunal to the point where the act on cooperation with the Tribunal might be annulled. I would not say that such a possibility is being discussed but it remains to be a very realistic option in case the indictments we talked about are really going to be issued." My question, sir, is simply: Are those your words?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that interview with precision, and I can't tell you with certainty whether I said that or not, since this has been carried by Mr. Banac I think, but it would be much easier for me to comment if I had the interview from Vecernji List.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Unfortunately sir, I don't have them at my fingertips all the dailies from Zagreb dating back even to 1998. If we had the Vecernji List, if I'd been able to get it on short notice, I promise you that we would have had that in front of you instead of this particular article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic perhaps you could approach the question this way: Is the quote in substance what you might have said, if not in actual accurate wording? Is it in substance -- is it in substance something that you might have said?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what my position was at the time regarding cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal, Your Honour, if that would satisfy you or the question put by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just very briefly, very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, my personal position was, as I said a moment ago, that we felt that the International Criminal Tribunal is not competent for the military operations Storm and Flash. And the government of the Republic of Croatia engaged in legal activities to deny the competence of the Tribunal by legal means. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that was your advice to the President of the Republic, Mr. Tudjman: "Don't recognise the competence of the Tribunal to investigate this particular matter"? Is that what you told him?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: What I have just said regarding my position was also the position shared by a large majority of Members of Parliament in Croatia. And this was nothing unknown. I don't remember that I put my position to President Tudjman precisely in those terms, but there were no secrets about it. I can't remember any specific situation when I needed to tell the President that, but in any event, that was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's interesting to me, sir, that you are a sitting member of the parliament which, as you said in your direct, is one branch of the government, that being the legislative branch but that at the same time, you are an inner circle, high level adviser to President Tudjman, who was of course running a different branch of your government, that being the executive. I want to ask you -- I'm asking you this now in your capacity as an adviser to President Tudjman. It was your advice, sir, as an adviser on internal or home affairs, that the Tribunal or that the Republic of Croatia should not cooperate with the Tribunal on this issue?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I have already said. For me personally, at the time, the question of breaking off relations did not arise, for me personally, and I repeat, that was my position then and still is today, that through means of law, the competence of the International Tribunal should have been questioned through a procedure that is permissible by international law, and that we should try to present arguments to show that the International Criminal Tribunal has no competence over the operations Storm and Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, one of the Croatian generals that we are talking about, I believe, is a gentleman named Gotovina. Do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in fact, Mr. Gotovina has been indicted by this Tribunal and he's currently a fugitive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to this question, because according to Rule 90, paragraph(H), the cross-examination must be limited to the topics covered by the examination-in-chief. I don't see what General Ante Gotovina has to do with Mr. Pasalic's testimony during the examination in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you see that I don't wish to object and I haven't objected often in the cross-examination, because I understand the tactics. It is important to put the right question rather than to wait for the answer, but it is true that we have to observe the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecutor is going outside the examination-in-chief, and they use as a pretext the credibility of the witness. So all these questions up to now have nothing to do with the questions put to the witness during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, the President at least once a week gives you a lecture on the difference between cross-examination and re-examination. And let me try and see if collectively we can tell you the difference. In cross-examination, one can ask any questions that go to credibility and relevance, and they are not confined to the questions raised in direct examination. In re-examination, you can only raise issues that have been raised in cross-examination. So, Mr. Seric, and Mr. Krsnik, we should not need to tell you that again. The issue is relevance. And if the Trial Chamber rules that the issue is irrelevant, it doesn't matter whether it was raised. If it's irrelevant, it stays irrelevant. But if the question is relevant, anything can be asked in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe in this case, the witness has answered this question and we are waiting for the following up questions raised by the Prosecution in this direction. Later on, we will know whether this question is relevant to the subject matter of this issue or not. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the transcript, I wish to convey my position. When I was cross-examining, I was not allowed to put questions that were beyond the scope of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President if I could just -- the rule which counsel have cited explicitly says that the cross shall be limited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, we are not discussing legal matters at this moment. You may proceed with your question. We are waiting for your follow-up questions on this very issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, my last question was whether in fact you know that Mr. Gotovina has been indicted by this Tribunal and that he's currently a fugitive, that is he's on the run. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I know that there -- an indictment has been issued against General Gotovina and the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's been reported, sir, that you spoke with him shortly before he disappeared last July. When is the last time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I don't exactly remember the date. I think it was last summer. Whether it was May or June, I don't know. It's very hard for me to recall the exact date. But it was last summer in May or in June, and that is when I saw General Gotovina last.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I saw him in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know his whereabouts today, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know his present whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the cross-examination continues to follow this course, I'm really worried as to how am I going to invite witnesses here? Because these are not examinations. These are investigations. I bring my factual witnesses and then they are investigated by the Prosecution. That's what investigative organs are for and if the Prosecution continues to examine my witnesses in this way, then I really don't know what is the point of a cross-examination. They had six years for this indictment and everything they are asking now is absolutely irrelevant to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Stringer is going to change the subject of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I've got one last question on this point, Mr. President with your permission, and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that related to the credibility of this witness? Or attitude of this witness to this it Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Knowing your views in respect to the Tribunal's competence to investigate or Prosecutor Storm and Flash, is it your view, sir, that Mr. Gotovina should turn himself into the Tribunal or should he remain a fugitive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, objection. Irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Skip this question, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic you have also criticised this Tribunal's finding in the Kordic decision which was handed down a year or so ago. It's been reported that you said that I think that this sentence, that is the sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stringer I think it's fluff to say he criticised the Kordic decision. He should not say anything more and we should move on and secondly Kordic is under appeal, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's under appeal, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think we should move on. If he agrees that he criticised Kordic, that's as far as we need to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me put this question to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can you please show me a document or a statement about Kordic's case? I would like to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me just first ask you and then we will show you. I think that's how Judge Clark would prefer to proceed. Did you criticise the Kordic judgement as being absolutely political, a political decision?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I was dissatisfied personally with such a decision but I don't remember precisely what I said, but personally I was not happy with that decision, and that was my position vis-a-vis that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 868.1. For the ELMO, please. It's a letter dated 25 August, 1999. While we are looking for that one, Dr. Pasalic, I'll ask you a lead-up question on this. I don't have this one in the Croatian language. Dr. Pasalic, in August, 1999, when you were an adviser to President Tudjman on domestic affairs, did the President of this Tribunal in fact complain to the UN Security Council about the non-cooperation of Croatia in respect of Storm and Flash but also in respect of Croatia's refusal to transfer Mladen Naletilic to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was the President's adviser for internal affairs and as for your question, I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would ask when the witness is being shown documents that we need a translation in Croatian for the witness to see it. This document has no translation into Croatian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning, I think the Prosecution asked about the knowledge of English of this witness, and this witness told us that he could understand English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour I didn't ask the witness about the document in any event. I asked him if he recalls whether, in fact, this was reported to the Security Council. I believe he testified that he doesn't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we had better hear from the witness. Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already replied, and I can say that I do not recall that objection that was addressed to the Security Council. There may have been such an objection, such a complaint, but I do not recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that you were not involved in the formation of Croatia's policy in respect of the Tribunal during the years that you were an adviser to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. That is not what I'm saying. As an adviser, I did have the opportunity to present my position and partly influence as an adviser and as a deputy -- as a member of government -- of parliament, I could influence the policy and there are a number of people who could present their views and to a certain extent influence the policy of the Republic of Croatia vis-a-vis cooperation with the International Tribunal. But the final decision in every specific case was made by the government of the Republic of Croatia because the government of the Republic of Croatia according to our constitutional law is competent and has the jurisdiction to make all the relevant decisions with regard to the International Criminal Tribunal, together with the government, there were other advisory bodies which could state their opinion but the final decision was always made by the government of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the final decision of the government, sir, in respect at least to Storm and Flash and also the transfer of Mr. Naletilic to the Tribunal, those are both positions that were supported by you, I take it? You were against the investigation on Storm and Flash?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. This is wrong. I was not against investigations. I was against the competence, i.e., I believed that there were convincing legal arguments to the effect -- corroborating the thesis that the International Criminal Tribunal is not competent to judge the military operations carried out during the operations Storm and Flash. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you issue a press release from The Hague yesterday that in fact you'd be testifying in these proceedings today? You've been quoted in the media today as having issued a press release from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. I did not watch the Croatian media, I did not read the Croatian media because they are not available here. What press release are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's one of the dailies in Zagreb. I don't have it in front of me, sir. It was just shown to me at the break. Have you made any statements publicly about your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: During the break, I was on my own in the witness room. I have not received any documents or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just want to put forth an objection. My -- my usual objection is that the witness should be approached correctly. HINA is not a daily and the Prosecutor has that document and he could have shown it to the witness. HINA is a news agency, a Croatian news agency like Reuters, and when he examines the witness first he tells him it's a daily and then he fails to show him the press release and we know he has it because he has shown it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, you have to ask this witness a very simple question: Did you issue the press release? It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll ask you again, witness, I'll repeat the question, I'll just read it again from the transcript. Did you issue a press release from The Hague yesterday that in fact you'd be testifying in these proceedings today?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. I did do that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did do you that, sir, because you view your testimony here today as in the nature of a political statement being given for the benefit of your constituents back in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No absolutely not. I came to testify for the benefit of the truth upon the invitation of the Defence. I wanted to testify and I wanted to say this Honourable Court the truth about the topics that I'm going to be asked about. And not for any political reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions about the presidential transcripts that you've talked about on your direct examination. My recollection, sir, is that there were certain times of meetings for which it was the normal, customary practice, to record. Those would be meetings involving international people, or also meetings, I believe, in which President Tudjman was acting as a statesman or in his capacity as a statesman with a group of people.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I was very precise and allow me to repeat that: There were meetings which were as a rule recorded. Those were the meetings between the President of the Republic with international officials, and those were meetings presided by the President of the Republic, and those were state bodies, such as the Defence counsel -- and counsel for the defence and security. So these meetings were recorded and everything else was -- differed from one occasion to another. The meetings of us who worked in the office as a rule were not recorded because we had dozens of conversations every day and what was recorded regularly were the meetings that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right. I understand that you drew a distinction between meetings that you've just described as opposed to the tete-a-tete type meetings, one on one, which were not transcribed or taped. Is that a correct distinction for me to draw?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. This is not correct. I believe that your conclusion is wrong, i.e., it is incomplete. What I wanted to say was that for some types of meetings that I've mentioned and those were international meetings and meetings of advisory or state bodies of the president, the practice was that they were regularly recorded. It was also customary not to record working meetings of the people who worked in the Office of the President. This is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Sir, do you recall that at various times in 1993, 1994, 1995, even later, delegation would come, Bosnian Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, would come as a delegation and would be received by President Tudjman in Zagreb for meetings? Do you know that to be true?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I take it that those meetings would fall into the international category of meetings for which it would have been normal procedure to tape record?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: These meetings certainly were international meetings, but earlier on, when I mentioned international meetings, what I had in mind were the meetings of the President of the Republic with the representatives of western states in various -- which were held in various contexts. They were either -- either meetings with peace mediators or high state officials of foreign states so I did not -- I did not -- I didn't mean these meetings, but the meetings that belonged to that category with those people, yes, there were such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You did participate in meetings between President Tudjman and the Bosnian Croat delegation, isn't that true? On a number of occasions during the years 1993 through even 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: It is very hard for me to say anything precisely about 1993, 1995, 1997. Yes, I did attend some of these meetings but it is very difficult for me to recall whether I attended a meeting in -- a meeting in 1993. There were no strict rules that one of the advisers was supposed to be present at all the meetings. This depended on the decision of the President of the Republic, and his opinion whether the presence of a certain adviser was required at a certain meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The tape recording procedure, sir, it sounds to me as though it was something that President Tudjman in fact desired to have in place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Recording of these meetings was obviously something that the President of the Republic had to decide and want.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It was being done for his benefit, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it was done for his benefit, but the President of the Republic was the person who was authorised to set up such a request, or issue such an order to the personnel that a certain meeting was to be recorded, and the President of the Republic certainly used these documents in discharging his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's for that reason, sir, that it was very important that the transcripts be an accurate reflection of the conversation that in fact took place. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether meetings with the Bosnian Croat delegation were tape recorded or not?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly. I would assume that some of them were recorded but I do not have any direct knowledge dating back to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Show the witness PT 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic we are going to it take you to one of the transcripts that has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Not sure if PT 14 is in the binder or not. I've got a clean copy, Mr. President, that I can give the usher. It doesn't have any markings on it. In fact, what I'll do is separate the English translation from the original language, the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic this is a transcript of a meeting that took place in the presidential palace on the 10th of November, 1993. What I'd first like to do is to direct you to certain parts of it where your name appears and then hopefully to refresh your recollection as to whether you were in fact present during this meeting. And I'm going to do that by referring you to the reference numbers that appear on the top right-hand corner of that document. The top, right-hand corner contains a reference number. I think the first page is R, if I can direct to you R 0157037, can you find that page number in your version?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have located the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you see your name appearing as one of the people speaking on this particular page?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Some of the other names appearing here are those of Jadranko Prlic, the President of the Republic, and also Dr. Mate Granic.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I see on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then on the next page, ending with the digits 038, you see your name there? This is all again in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your name appears again on page 50? 050?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is on page 050.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a meeting, as I mentioned, Dr. Tudjman, Mate Granic, yourself, Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic, and I believe some others. Do you recall attending meetings with Mr. Boban and Mr. Prlic in the presidential palace?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I remember that I did attend some meetings with Mr. Boban and Mr. Prlic but I'm not sure that this was this exactly this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's discuss some of the points raised in this and perhaps it will refresh your recollection. I want to take you first, sir, in your version, to the page ending with the numbers 7021, English reference is page number R0183340. Ending digits 3340. Dr. Pasalic, as I mentioned, this is a meeting held on the 10th of November, 1993. What's being discussed here is a recent military operation of the HVO in a place called Stupni Do where is located in the municipality of Varos, Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I want to take you to a statement by President Tudjman, where he says, "Let's move on to your problems. Who is that Ivica Rajic of yours?" Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then continuing, he's being informed by Mr. Boban who Ivica Rajic is. Continuing on to the next page. President Tudjman asks,"When was Stupni Do?" Mr. Boban responds, "The 24th." And then continuing on now, the page ending 342, in the English version, 024 in your version, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tudjman says, "Dear friends, you're being in question, you are bringing into question the position of Croatia and not only yours with such actions as happened with Stupni Do." Now, are you aware, sir, that Stupni Do is the location of a massacre of Bosnian Muslim civilians that occurred in late October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I must admit I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know that in Stupni Do, on the 23rd and 24th of October, 1993, units of the HVO under the command of Ivica Rajic massacred Bosnian Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I remember that in the media, there were reports about the problem of Stupni Do but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall discussing that incident in the presidential palace with Dr. Tudjman and the others as indicated in this transcript?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this particular meeting, and I don't remember attending such a meeting at which this problem was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, did you keep notes of the meetings that you attended with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Mostly no, those were just daily notes, when I needed to write something upon instructions from the President. It was a daily memo, a reminder for the next day or the next few days but for no other purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So all you have to go on is your memory, then, you don't remember anything else about these meetings with President Tudjman and other members of the Bosnian Croat delegation?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're not in a position, sir, to say one way or the other whether these transcripts such as the one we are looking at are in fact authentic transcripts of tape recordings of meetings that took place on the dates indicated?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak about all the transcripts because certainly there may be events and dates and topics which I would recall. Regarding this one I have in front of me, I truly cannot remember that I attended any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Continuing back to the transcript, page -- ending 343 in the English version and for you, sir, I think it's the same page ending with the digits 024. President Tudjman says, talking about the latest issue of Newsweek, "I appointed you there and that is the policy of Croatia over there." Now, sir, my question is this: In fact, when he's talking about who he appointed, he's talking about Mate Boban, and when he's talking about the policy of Croatia, he's talking about the policy of Croatia in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. I think you misunderstood the context. If you're quoting this particular sentence from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just then to continue on, sir: Pages 028 to 029 of your version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise but again there is a misinterpretation in the cross-examination. The facts are being distorted. It doesn't say Newsweek anywhere in the Croatian original. It's not there. This can just be guess work. I'm over there AAS. That is the Croatian original. And I don't know where the Prosecutor found Newsweek because it doesn't say that in the Croatian original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In the English translation of course we saw the words Newsweek. But any way it's a matter of translation. We will ask the professional interpreters to look into this matter. But that's not an important issue, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, but we don't need an interpreter to read the Croatian original. We really don't need an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for drawing our attention to that point. We will do that at a later stage. You may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that events like Stupni Do and then subsequently the destruction of the old bridge, the Stari Most in Mostar, are what led to the criticism and ultimately the resignation of Mate Boban as president of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: With reference to Mr. Mate Boban, the late Mr. Mate Boban, the context of his resignation is completely a different one. Mr. Boban resigned on the eve of the achievement of the peace accords in Washington, when as far as I know, the international -- representatives of the international community demanded that Mr. Boban withdraw because he was thought to be an unacceptable symbol for achieving a peace agreement at the beginning of 1994, and it was directly requested of Mr. Tudjman that he bring his influence to bear for Mr. Boban to withdraw as he was considered to be an obstacle to reaching an agreement. So that was the background and the context within which Mr. Mate Boban resigned. This negotiating within the context of the negotiating process for a peace settlement in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So Mr. Boban resigned because Mr. Tudjman brought his own influence to bear and decided that he would not support Mr. Boban staying in that position?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't say that you are right. Mr. Boban could have not resigned. It was up to his own political judgement as to how he would behave. What I do know is that there were requests that Mr. Tudjman influence Mr. Boban, but the final decision was up to Mr. Boban, whether he would make such a move or not. Obviously, it was his judgement at the time that though I know that he believed that that request was unfounded, he resigned so as not to be an obstacle, though he didn't feel that he was an obstacle, as far as I can remember. He did that because this was required of him, concessions, if concessions are being required of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then at the same time, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic as a symbol of Muslim policies, or Mr. Silajdzic should also resign because otherwise it was felt that the pressure was being brought to bear unilaterally on Croatia only, on the Croats only, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Tudjman used his influence and Mr. Boban resigned. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I think that that is simplifying things. Relations were far more complex and the times were far more difficult and more complex. It is difficult to give a proper picture of them in such a simplified -- in such simplified terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the transcript. Your version, sir, the Croatian version, the pages ending 028 and 029, the English, 346 and 347, in the English 346, President Tudjman says, and they are talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted my learned friend to complete his question but since you are giving me the chance to object, I object because it has to do with the transcript, namely the question relates to a transcript of an alleged meeting that the witness does not recollect, and any further insistence and examination on it, in my view, is quite inappropriate. How can one insist on a witness commenting on something that he does not remember? Only if the Prosecution wishes here in public to read something from these transcripts for the benefit of the Croatian media, something that may possibly suit him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, those meetings happened about seven or eight years ago. Nobody has a long memory to remember everything, every detail of a certain meeting. I believe the Prosecutor is trying his best to refresh the memory of this witness. We have to give the Prosecutor a chance to do that. And later on, we'll assess the testimony given by this witness at a later stage. Yes, Mr. Stringer. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic I want to direct you now to it a passage of the President where he says, "You will now issue an order that he has been replaced and send him, if there is fighting going on now, for Gornji Vakuf send him over there to fight, right away not quietly, instead give a statement, inform UNPROFOR and UNHCR." Now, Mr. Pasalic, my question is this: He's talking about Ivica Rajic and dealing with him because he's being held responsible for the events at Stupni Do. Do you recall discussing this matter? Do you recall being present when this was discussed, what to do with Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that in fact, President Tudjman did have the authority, as indicated here, to direct the Bosnian Croat leadership to take specific action with respect to military members of the HVO? He had the authority to direct that Rajic be replaced, that he be sent to Gornji Vakuf, and that statements be issued informing the internationals of that fact?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I think that you're absolutely wrong. President Tudjman had no authority to replace anyone or to order the replacement of anyone within the units outside the units of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then continuing on the next page of the English, I believe for you, Dr. Pasalic, your page 029, they are discussing the fact that he is going to be accused as a war criminal, that is Ivica Rajic, and the fact that merely replacing him is not enough, that it's necessary to institute proceedings. And there is an a passage here three-quarters of the way down the English version by Dr. Granic saying, "It's very important to say that. I think it facilitates matters. That is a court inquiry." So again, isn't this, sir, the leadership of Croatia discussing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, may it please the Court, the Prosecution is not trying to refresh this witness's recollection any longer. He has not been for the last five to ten minutes, and I apologise for being on my feet, but I speak English fluently and my lead counsel does not. But Your Honour, Mr. Stringer is no longer trying to refresh the recollection of this witness. This witness has stated several times he does not recall this meeting, Mr. Stringer is simply directing the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, don't given any hints to this witness. I have already said that we will give another chance to the Prosecutor to refresh the memory of this witness. We could arrive at a conclusion about the testimony of this witness at a late later stage. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic speaking today, now, many years after all of these events, do you know that in fact there was an incident a military operation, at Stupni Do in October of 1993? Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I know that there were some casualties there, but the actual circumstances, I don't know. I know that there were casualties and this was reported in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You don't know that Ivica Rajic was indicted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: There were several Rajics. There were various men mentioned with the same surname. So that I'm not quite sure whether it was Ivica Rajic. I know that the surname Rajic did appear frequently in the media, because if I may just add a sentence or two about these surnames, in the Croatian media, every so often there is a report that somebody has been indicted or will be indicted and there are hundreds of names appearing. So that in this host of names in the media, during the past few years, it is difficult to remember whether it was Ivica Rajic or some other Rajic because in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were several people with that same surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next passage I want to take you to, sir, is on your page ending 7031. The English ending 348. The bottom of 348. This is the President again speaking. "So that we have on one hand a firmly organised government, and accordingly, the entire structure of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna with its tasks and the military, which I sent down there. You know that I sent a new commander and ordered that new volunteers be sent to defend the Vitez line, that is to say Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak and to bring this Gornji Vakuf to an end and later Bugojno." Now, sir, my question to you is whether this is in fact a true statement, that at this very time, in early November, 1993, President Tudjman did send a new commander down to take over the HVO, Ante Roso, who went down there and replaced Slobodan Praljak. Do you know that to have taken place?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that it took place but what I'm quite certain of is that President Tudjman could not send anyone, order anyone, nor did he do so on any occasion with respect to events outside Croatia. If certain soldiers or officers went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, they did so certainly on the basis of their own decision. In most cases, these were people who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina and who, because of the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina, went there as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in fact, President Tudjman says right here that he ordered new volunteers be sent to defend the Vitez line. Do you know in fact -- do you know in fact, sir, that Ante Roso replaced Slobodan Praljak during this period of time as commander of the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: With respect to your first question, I just wish to add, and assert, that I'm certain that President Tudjman did not send any volunteers to Bosnia-Herzegovina. If somebody is a volunteer, he goes on his own. No one needs to send him there. And as for Mr. Roso, I don't know whether -- or rather if he was there, then his going there was not following orders of the President of the Republic but on his own free will, on his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you aren't completely informed on all these matters sir it's because military affairs was in fact not within your area of competence, as you testified on direct. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. I said very clearly that my duties within the Office of the President of the Republic, as adviser, did not cover military matters in the strict sense but sending soldiers or officers to another country is a political issue in every sense, and if it had taken place, I would certainly be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that men in Croatia who refused to go fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina were prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of any such cases, that in such cases, that you are referring to, if any, first of all, I don't know of any such cases and still less do I know that any kind of court proceedings were conducted against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that Ante Roso was a general of the Croatian Army before he went down to take command over the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Roso was a member of the Croatian Army, but I don't know exactly in which period of time he had which rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I direct you, sir, to Exhibit 654.2? It's in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the next question, to avoid interruption, I would like to ask the Prosecutor to tell us whether it is a new exhibit, and it says, "Source," and it says Anto Nobilo. Could the Prosecutor tell us who Anto Nobilo is, who provided him with this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, this is an exhibit from the Blaskic trial, the reference to Mr. Nobilo is Defence attorney for Mr. Blaskic and this document was provided by Mr. Blaskic's attorney during the course of the Blaskic proceedings and admitted into evidence in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, my question, this is a document dated 20 October, 1993, some 20 days before the meeting in Zagreb that we have just been talking about. Over the signature of brigadier Miljenko Crnjac. This indicates that on the 15th of October, 1993 Major General Ante Roso submitted a request to leave for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that his request was granted. Sir, does this assist you in recalling the time frame in which Mr. Roso took command of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document is Exhibit 793.01. Sir, this is dated 23 February, 1995. This is General Roso's request for re-engagement in the Croatian Army. Do you know, sir, whether he rejoined the Croatian Army on or about February of 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And during the intervening period, sir, that is the period of time when Ante Roso was not a member of the Croatian Army, isn't it true, sir, that he was commanding the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: What I do remember from that period is, I think, that Mr. Roso, with regard to duties linked to Sarajevo, if I remember correctly the period, that he had some military duties over there, but I really don't remember anything else with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Coming back to this passage that we were just reading from, besides the comment or the statement in which President Tudjman says that I sent down there, I sent a new commander, it says he also ordered new volunteers be sent to these places, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, those are all located in central Bosnia, isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Despite whatever de jure powers the President may have had under your constitution, sir, isn't it true that President Tudjman had, in effect, the power to deploy units of the HV, the Croatian Army, into Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: The President had no authority along those lines, and it is quite certain that President Tudjman did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, at the time that the international community in fact had concluded otherwise, and was subjecting President Tudjman and his government to intense criticism for their involvement in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: From that period of time, I do remember that there were some criticisms of that kind. I also remember from meetings with representatives of the international community their opinion that the Bosnian Muslims or rather Mr. Izetbegovic had launched an offensive against the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because there was a large concentration of the Muslim population, that had been expelled from occupied areas of eastern Bosnia and their judgement was that Mr. Izetbegovic had reneged on some earlier peace proposals and arrangements --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I was asking you about this specific issue, which is the involvement or the presence of the Croatian Army. Time is a bit limited and so if you'll forgive me I needed to cut you off. Mr. Krsnik can ask you about the offensive that you've just mentioned in his redirect if he wishes to do so. Could you look at Exhibit IAC82? It's the third exhibit from the end in the binder. Now this is an United Nations document, sir. I have it in English and French. I don't have it in your language. Sir, this is a letter dated 1 February 1994, from the Secretary-General of the United Nations to the President of the UN Security Council. IAC82, third from the end. You've got it. I apologise, sir, if you're not able to read the English text. I'm just going to read you a very short passage from this letter. In the third paragraph. "As the offensives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government forces against the HVO have become successful, the numbers of Croatian soldiers appear to have increased. It is assessed that in total there is the equivalent of three Croatian brigades of regular army personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina, approximately 3.000 to 5.000. This is an estimation." Sir, now, as indicated in this letter and also in the transcript here which is a conversation taking place in November of 1993, isn't it true that as a result of military successes of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, President Tudjman found it necessary to send additional units of the HV, the Croatian Army, into Bosnia-Herzegovina to support units of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: That is quite certainly incorrect. This period, February, 1994, was the period just before the achievement of the Washington peace agreement and all the activities of the President of the Republic at the time, as far as I know, were focused on achieving a peace agreement rather than assisting and fanning the conflict. This is quite the opposite to what President Tudjman was doing. You probably know that it was thanks to the President's efforts that a peace was achieved and the Washington Agreement signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic, I want to take you now to, in the Croatian language version, back to the transcript, page ending 0 -- I'm sorry, 7031, page ending 349 in the English version. We could just take the transcript out of the binder. I think it would -- because we are going to move around a little bit more. It's the Croatian language version. Dr. Pasalic you've got a piece of paper in front of you. I want to direct you to the text that surrounds the name Zulfo Robovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your page 7032 perhaps. Do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The top part of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. While we are doing this, perhaps I could ask the usher to pull 666.2 which is going to be the next exhibit. Just to save some time. What's happening, Mr. Pasalic or Dr. Pasalic in this part of the transcript is that a number of persons are being proposed and discussed to form the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and this discussion begins with President Tudjman saying, "Let's follow a set order. What kind of proposals do you have for the government?" And then Mr. Prlic speaks, this is on page 349 of the English, "Renewal and development, that's a ministry. Renewal and development, Zulfo Robovic." And President Tudjman asks a little about him. Where is he from? What does he do? And said -- there is further discussion. And then moving across to page 7035 on your version, 353 in the English, there is another person discussed, proposed to take over the ministry on agriculture, water resources management, forestry, Marko Bozanovic. And then a few lines down, there is the name of Ilija Kozen for traffic and communication, Ilija Zuljevic for employment, social and family welfare. Now, Dr. Pasalic I want to ask you whether you recall whether in fact those gentlemen were approved by President Tudjman and their positions in the government as indicated here were in fact announced publicly on that day? And I'm going to take you to Exhibit 666.2.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: What I can say about this is just to repeat what I have said before, and that is that I don't remember this it particular meeting. I can only say that President Tudjman never appointed, nor did he indeed have any authority to appoint, any officials from the ranks of the Croatian people and that is all. The decision on that, decisions on that were made by the competent body of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether these people were appointed or not is something that I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to put it to you, the report that's now in front of you, and that's also on the ELMO, is a report from -- that's been picked up -- issued by the Zagreb Radio Croatia on the 10th of November, 1993, same day as this meeting. And this report is in fact the announcement of the selection of the government members. And some of the names appearing on this report are the very names that are being mentioned in this transcript, Marko Bozanovic, Zulfo Robovic, Ilija Zuljevic, my question to you, sir, is whether in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, I'm sorry to interrupt you but could you tell me how long you're going to take for this cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's going to take me more than five minutes, Mr. President. I think that I can -- I think that I'm going to need to use all the time that's been allotted, which I think is at least an hour and 55 minutes. I think that takes us beyond 7.00, and I'm in your hands, Mr. President. We are drawing to the very end of the transcript. I'm certain that we can conclude on the transcript today, and then beyond that, there are a couple of additional items which I think are of interest to the Trial Chamber relating to some of the questions raised by Judge Clark on -- during the direct in respect of some of the inquiries in Zagreb on the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The problem is that we run out of tapes. I've been informed by the radio booths that they have to have one minute break so that they can change the tapes, right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, my proposal would then be to continue tomorrow, Mr. President, but again, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let us stop. Let us wait for one minute and then we'll hear what Mr. Krsnik will tell us. We wanted to have everything recorded in the tapes. Well, I think we need some consultations to see whether we can continue our sittings after 7.00 because the interpreters have been working for almost two hours. They deserved to have a break and we also want to know whether the accused, Mr. Naletilic, is okay to continue for maybe 30 minutes more after 7.00. So we'll break now for 20 minutes to see the results from the consultations with your client, Mr. Krsnik, and with the interpreters, with the Registrar. We'll resume at 7.20. Yes, Witness? Do you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can just -- my request -- I have a request, when you're deciding this matter. Tomorrow preparations start for the new parliamentary session and if at all possible, I would have to be in the parliament tomorrow, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have already taken your request into consideration and we will conduct the consultations during the break. We'll resume at 20 past 7.00. --- Break taken at 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, did you talk with your client about his health?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is your client ready to be with us for another 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have to remember that this Trial Chamber has done superhuman effort to accommodate the request of this witness to sit at this late hour. So we have to finish this witness in 30 minutes. Yes, Mr. Stringer. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic just one more short series of questions about this transcript we have been looking at. One last name I want to direct your attention to. Beginning, sir, the Croatian language version, page 035 to 036. English version ending with the digits 353.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can I maybe assist my learned friend? What transcript are we talking about? Which PT numbers, we don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's the same one, PT 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic I just wanted to ask if you can find the name, there is a reference to a Dr. Vladimir Simunovic from Sarajevo. Do you see his name on the page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, on page 35 at the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you'll just follow along with me, what's happening here is that Jadranko Prlic again is mentioning names of persons proposed for different positions, and as we see here, Dr. Vladimir Simunovic is proposed to be the Minister of Health. The President asks, "What is he doing now?" Prlic says, "He's one of the best known neurosurgeons." Passing to the next page in the English version, the President asks, a couple lines down, "Who is your chief of the health service now?" Prlic says, "Bagaric. Do you know him?" The President says, "I do. He even came to Zagreb and was very active in Zagreb and in regard to everything. Why couldn't he hold the post?" Prlic responds, "He's in the medical corps of the Main Staff." Again, continuing, passing to the next page in the English now, 355, there is a reference here to a statement made by you, "That would be in the political and organisational respect." Prlic says, "I absolutely have nothing against that. He is the representative." And then going down, Granic says, "Excellent continuity, in cooperation I mean." Prlic says, "So we are going ahead with Bagaric. We will have to change this one down there, two Bagarics especially from Tomislavgrad." And then passing to the next page in the English version, 356, Dr. Pasalic, this statement is attributed to you. "Beside Mate and you he is the most prominent person from those fields in the Croatian media." Prlic then says, "Then it will have to be done." Now, Dr. Pasalic, my question is whether this again is evidence that in fact President Tudjman played a leading role in the selection of persons who were to hold positions in the Bosnian -- excuse me, in the government of the Croatian Republic or Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Initially someone was proposed, Dr. Tudjman indicated that he favoured Bagaric, and then it was Bagaric who was agreed.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: What I can tell you with regard to your opinion is that President Tudjman certainly did not engage in the appointment of officials in the governmental bodies of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. His influence was mostly at some critical moments when major events were taking place, first and foremost within the peace process, and on the request of the top representatives of the international community. I am positive when I say that President Tudjman would never deal in issues such as who would hold the post of health minister, agriculture minister and other such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Taking you back, sir, to Exhibit 666.2, which is the press release from Zagreb Radio dated the same day as this transcript, again, sir, we found the name Bagaric as being identified as the person who will take the Ministry of health. Are you able to find his name on that document?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it would seem to me, sir, that this press release is an accurate reflection of what actually happened in this meeting. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we all have this document in front of us. This is not the Zagreb Radio. And the source here is east European unclassified, Radio Zagreb in Serbo-Croatian. This is certainly not Radio Zagreb in 1994, and here there is no evidence that this is a report by the Zagreb Radio. As far as I can see, this is the English daily report from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Who wrote this, who carried this? I don't know but this is not Radio Zagreb. I kept quiet. I waited until the end of the question, but again, I object because the witness is given a wrong interpretation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer maybe you can give us indications about the source of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the document is from an open source called FIBIS, which is a report that is made of -- in which the various media broadcasts are monitored, and written down in a number of languages. This is an open source that we regularly search and refer to when we are looking to find information about events. This is a FIBIS report which is based upon a media report from the Zagreb Radio Croatia network which is what's indicated on the top left-hand corner of this document dated 10 November, 1993, report by Zdrenko Vranjes original language, I'm sorry, Croatian network in Serbo-Croatian, 1800 GMT, which is the time, on the 10th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let us hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say anything specific, Mr. Prosecutor is drawing his own conclusions. Here I can see a number of names which are not mentioned in the transcript, and now when I looked at the transcript, I am more and more certain that I was never present at the meeting, although I said earlier on that I did not remember this meeting, but after so many details, I would certainly remember the meeting had I attended this meeting, because after all these details, and the host of names, I would have remembered had I been present at the meeting. And this thing that the Prosecution -- Prosecutor has presented does not mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, sir, as you testified you attended hundreds even thousands of meetings with President Tudjman. Isn't it a fact, sir, that you just aren't in a position to remember one way or another whether you were at this meeting? You have no notes, or at least you've brought no notes, nothing you can consult other than your memory.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. I cannot consult anything but my own memory, and this did indeed take place a long time ago, if it did take place in this way. I told you that I do not believe that this happened in the -- in this way because President Tudjman did not interfere in appointment or resignations, save for the context of Mr. Mate Boban. After all these details, after reading the transcripts in more details, after all the things that you have mentioned, Mr. Prosecutor, I believe that I would remember had I attended this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Exhibit 876.001, please. Dr. Pasalic, on your direct examination, you talked about this inquiry related to the purchase of a newspaper, and I want to ask you some questions about that, just to clarify. It's my understanding, sir, that a transcript of a meeting between you and President Tudjman has been made public, the meeting said to have occurred on December 27th of 1997. In this meeting it's alleged that you discussed with President Tudjman the use of off-shore bank accounts in the Channel Islands, in the Caribbean, as part of an effort to surreptitiously purchase a newspaper called Vecernji List. The transcript, I believe, sir, is the one that you've testified about on your direct examination which you said that it was not accepted by the inquiry that was appointed to look into this matter. Do you remember that testimony? Are we talking about the same incident?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, it's your position, and it's been your assertion in the media, I see, that you assert that the tape or the transcript in which this recording or discussion is alleged to have occurred, this transcript is not accurate or that it's a fictitious transcript; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The allegation that you were involved in an attempt to surreptitiously purchase the newspaper called Vecernji List is a very serious allegation which could subject you potentially to criminal investigation. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. This is not correct, because the fictitious transcript -- so-called transcripts were seriously considered first by the parliamentary commission and then the -- a judiciary body and they both established that the document was not authentic. It was not accepted as evidence in that procedure, and it was established subsequently that in the privatisation of the newspaper that you're referring to, there were no irregularities. This is -- this was thoroughly investigated from -- by the Croatian judiciary system, and this process was finalised a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you bring any papers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can it be allowed for this document to be read and can we hear the source of this document? Again, this is not a newspaper article or -- but excerpts from something, and we don't know where from, who from, whether it -- what newspaper it is. So we don't know anything about this piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, if you could?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The second of the two pages indicates the source which is the Sunday Times article dated June 18th, 2000. And again I'm happy to read it but the gist of the article is that there are indications based upon the transcript of 27 December, 1997, in which Doctor Pasalic explained how a smoke screen of companies would hide the President's role, the use of offshore funds in an attempt to surreptitiously purchase the Vecernji List.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Pasalic, my question to you is first: I'm not -- I don't have any papers on the ultimate findings of this commission, and I take it you haven't brought any with you. So at this stage we are just going to have to take your word in terms of the outcome or the findings of this commission.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: It is no problem at all to obtain the relevant documents. I don't have it on me obviously because I didn't know it would be of any interest to you. Otherwise I would have brought it with me but what is absolutely correct and what was published in the media and you can certainly access this data, if not, I will be only glad to send them to you so you will be able to find out that after several months of investigation, that these allegations were rejected as incorrect and that all the documents were handed over to the Croatian judicial organs whose decision was also published. The decision -- their ruling is final in the legal procedure. This ruling is known to everybody because it was published in the media, and as for this ruling, there was no irregularity in the privatisation of this particular newspaper which means that any prior article to the contrary is false.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were the focus or the subject of this investigation, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: No. This is not correct. I was one of the persons who testified before this commission, but there were a number of other officials who also testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, sir, it benefited you and it benefits you personally, then, if in fact the presidential transcripts or this particular one is discredited. Then you have a personal interest in seeing it discredited because of this inquiry.

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: This is not correct. There are -- is a number of other pieces of evidence for the possible crime, and in this particular case, it does not benefit my position in any way to discredit this or any other transcript. So this is -- so what you said is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if the transcript were true, sir, if it were an accurate statement, wouldn't that create some serious problems for you in respect of those allegations on the Vecernji List?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: This transcript was the subject of conversations, investigation, and it was clearly established that that particular transcript was not authentic. I don't know what else I could add to that. In addition to the transcript, as a possible argument, there was also debate on other things and evidence -- testimonies were given by others who had any information about the matter. Finally the proceedings were finalised and they did not -- they had not established any irregularities or illegal dealings, i.e. it was established that the sale had complied -- had been in compliance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I have just one moment to confer with my colleague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have to remind you that your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm just going to make sure that there isn't just one last point but I think I've finished, Mr. President. [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have one last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic I want to put this to you: Is it true that there have been reports in publications of another transcript which indicates that in October of 1999, you had a discussion with President Tudjman about possibly arranging for Mr. Naletilic to escape from the prison hospital he was being held in Zagreb? And on that day, and also on the 1st of October, 1999, you discussed various methods and strategies, legal and medical, that could be employed to delay or to prevent Mr. Naletilic from being transferred to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to when you say published in the media. I would like to see what was published in the media. What I can say is that I never discussed these issues with the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My last exhibit, Mr. President, I will just show it to the witness 876.002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic this is an article from Nacional dated the 12th of July, 2000 referring to audiotapes of a conversation between you and President Tudjman. Sir, are you familiar with these reports? Do you recall these reports when they came out, suggesting your involvement in an attempt to prevent Mr. Naletilic from being transferred to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: We have here the Croatian weekly Nacional against which I have raised charges before a Croatian court. This weekly has published thousands of negative pages about me. Very recently I have won in a court case against one of the journalists of this paper, who printed lies about me, and that's why the Court decided in my favour. Recently, a Prosecutor ex officio raised charges against the editor-in-chief of this paper because there is a reasonable grounds to suspect that he committed a crime in order to discredit me. So I don't remember this particular article because it is just a -- one in a host of articles that this weekly has published about me, and this weekly, as is well known in Croatia, is very close to the current President of the Republic, and that it may be considered a semi-official voice of the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour,, I don't wish to it take any more time

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These transcripts when we are talking about this newspaper, was this a typical example of fabrications by this weekly?

utterances.speaker: IVIC PASALIC
utterances.text: That weekly published a wide variety of fabrications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to object to leading questions on redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this late hour I think Mr. Krsnik is asking a question on the point. Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
